tagline.text: A shallow wreck off Coron Island, reduced to a bare skeleton, ideal for snorkeling

location.label: Location
location.text: Off the northwest coast of Coron Island, Palawan (reached by boat from Coron Town)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (one stop on an island-hopping tour)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,400~2,000 (per person on a joiner tour, lunch and most entrance fees included)

children.text: This roughly 25 m shipwreck off the northwest of Coron Island is nothing but a steel hull skeleton lying on a shallow seabed. The bow sits at about 5 m, so even snorkelers can see its whole outline, while the stern drops to about 22 m, which makes it popular with divers too.

Skeleton Wreck lies just off the northwest corner of Coron Island. As the name suggests, the wooden parts rotted away long ago, leaving only the keel, ribs and stringers of the steel hull standing like bones. At about

long, it is small compared with the large wrecks of Coron Bay. Many accounts call it a Japanese patrol boat or supply vessel, but the exact identity of the ship is said to be unconfirmed, so take any story a local guide tells you as a rough guide only.
When people talk about Coron's wrecks, they usually picture large Japanese warships lying around 30 m down, but Skeleton Wreck is a very different experience. The bow rests in shallow water about
from the shore at roughly
5m
, and the ship lies slanted along the coral slope, getting deeper toward the stern to about
. Snorkelers look down from the surface at the bones of the hull, the coral and schools of small fish, while divers choose their depth and swim around it.
The whole structure is thickly encrusted with coral and barnacles, so it now works like an artificial reef. On the starboard side of the hull, at about

, there is a pass-through from inside the boat out to the coral reef, which is divers' favorite spot. Lionfish, parrotfish, damselfish, stonefish and nudibranchs are often seen, and sea turtles are occasionally reported.
Most travelers visit as one stop on a Coron island-hopping tour (Tour B, Ultimate and similar). When the boat anchors over the wreck, you put on a life jacket, hop straight in and stay for about
30 minutes to 1 hour
, alternating with land-based highlights such as Kayangan Lake and Twin Lagoon. Being one of the few Coron wrecks you can enjoy with just a snorkel is its biggest appeal.

blocks.title: Wreck skeleton visible from the surface

children.text: With the bow at around
5m
, snorkeling alone is enough to see the rows of steel ribs. On clear days the outline of the whole hull is sharp, which also makes for good photos.

Coral and barnacles have grown thickly over the steel frame left after the wood rotted away, turning it into a small reef. Tropical fish such as damselfish, parrotfish and lionfish move through the structure.

On the starboard side of the hull there is a passage leading from inside the ship out to the coral reef. It is not a fully enclosed tunnel but an open structure between the ribs, so Open Water divers can pass through without much trouble.

blocks.title: Shallow to deep in one dive

children.text: One ship lies slanted from about
5m
at the bow to about
at the stern, so snorkelers, beginner divers and experienced divers can all see the same wreck at a depth that suits them.
You can observe small creatures such as stonefish and nudibranchs, and the occasional sea turtle. Reports say that when nearby boats feed the fish, large schools sometimes gather all at once.

blocks.title: An easy stop on the hopping route

children.text: It is part of the Tour B and Ultimate tours, so you can stop here without any diving gear. Unlike the stair trek down to Kayangan Lake, you get in the water straight from the boat, so it is easy on the legs.

The shallow depth and simple structure make it a good way to get used to wreck scenery before tackling Coron's big wrecks. You circle the outside rather than going deep inside the hull, so it is not demanding.

items.title: Scuba diving
items.subtitle: Half-day course with a dive center

children.text: Pick up gear and attend the briefing at a dive center in Coron Town.
Take the dive boat to the dive point off the northwest of Coron Island.
Descend to about
at the stern, look around the steel skeleton and the
starboard pass-through, then ascend slowly and look at the coral around the shallow bow.
After a surface interval, make a second dive at another site or finish for the day.
Have lunch and return to town.
Dive prices and the required certification (Skin Diver or Open Water) differ by center, so ask before booking.
The airport for the Coron area is Francisco B. Reyes Airport (USU, Busuanga Airport) on Busuanga Island.

The routes and departure airports for Manila to Busuanga change often with airline circumstances. In 2026, Cebgo reportedly moved its Manila flights from NAIA to Clark, and Sunlight Air was reported to fly from Clark to Busuanga twice a day. Check departure airports and schedules on the airline's site before booking.

Skeleton Wreck cannot be reached by land, only by boat. Use an island-hopping tour boat or a dive boat from the Coron Town pier.

Dive centers say the boat ride takes roughly 30 minutes to 1 hour, so confirm directly with your center.

3.5 hours
Fares published in February 2025 were roughly
one way, depending on the vessel and departure time. Check the latest fares and times locally.

Some sources say Skeleton Wreck can be visited all year, but because it is reached by boat, weather matters a great deal. The most reliable period is the November–May dry season, and the sea is calmest and clearest especially from December to April. December to March is also the busiest peak season, so aim for November or April–May if you want fewer people.

From June to October, the southwest monsoon and typhoons worsen sea conditions, and island-hopping tours are often canceled by coast guard warnings. Visibility is also reported to vary widely, from about 4 m to over 20 m, so if clear water matters to you, visit in the dry season.

rows: Peak season. Good visibility and few canceled tours. Book ahead.
Edges of the dry season, rain possible
Fewer tourists and relatively stable conditions.

Most people stay in Coron Town, where hopping-tour operators, dive centers and restaurants are concentrated, making getting around easy. Prices range from cheap guesthouses to resorts with sea views, so choose according to your budget and tour schedule. Book early in the peak season.

Lunch is often included on joiner tours. It is usually eaten on the boat or at a nearby beach, and the menu differs by operator. If your tour does not include lunch, you can reportedly have a simple meal at a local restaurant for about
. There are several restaurants and cafes in town, so have dinner there.
When booking a tour, check that Skeleton Wreck is actually on the itinerary rather than relying on the course name. Tour A and B contents differ by operator.
Ask in advance whether entrance fees, lunch and the environmental fee are included in the price. In some cases you must pay them separately in cash.
If you snorkel, always wear a life jacket, and since there are many places where your feet cannot touch the bottom, stay close to the guide if you are not a confident swimmer.
Bring a waterproof case or action camera for underwater photos. The shallow bow gets plenty of light and gives the best pictures.
It is more hygienic and convenient to bring your own mask. Rental costs about
Coral-covered iron structures are sharp, so do not grab or step on them, and keep your distance so you do not touch the hull.
The sun is strong, so pack reef-safe sunscreen and a rash guard. Avoid sunscreens containing ingredients that harm coral.
Diving requires Open Water certification or higher, and the deep stern section calls for experience. Talk to your center and decide on a depth.
The wreck has corroded iron and many gaps, so even in shallow water there is a risk of snagging or scraping yourself. Do not enter the hull and follow your guide's instructions.
On days with bad sea conditions, island-hopping tours can be canceled by coast guard warnings, so leave slack in your schedule during the rainy season.
Visibility varies greatly with weather and currents, from about 4 m to over 20 m. You may not see as much as you hoped.
The Coron Bay area is part of the Coron Island Protected Area and a traditional fishing ground of the Tagbanwa people. Do not leave trash, and do not touch or feed corals and marine life.
Fees, entrance charges and rules change often. Check the latest announcements, and get a receipt and a list of inclusions instead of relying on verbal promises.
For scuba diving, stay within a depth that suits your certification and condition, and check your insurance and equipment before you dive.
